title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
rationale: The source found misinformation shared 18.2 points less than true/neutral content (95% CI [-20.4,-16.0]), but respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more (p<0.001), a tertile contrast that was underpowered and US-English only. This design pre-selects belief in disputed claims as the moderator, stratifies on it and on survey language (English/Spanish), and tests one registered interaction.
contribution: Tests whether the misinformation sharing penalty shrinks among high-belief respondents and whether it generalizes to Spanish-language samples.
limitations: Interaction power is lower than main-effect power; language subgroup effects are exploratory.
Belief tertiles are measured, not randomized, so the moderator may bundle correlated traits.
Single-headline sharing intent differs from the source forced-choice pair design.

design.title: Headline type by belief in disputed claims and survey language
design.overview: Respondents first complete a belief-in-disputed-claims scale. They are then randomized to see a true/neutral or a false headline, and report sharing intent and plausibility. Recruitment is stratified by belief tertile and by language (English or Spanish).
design.hypothesis: The gap in sharing between misinformation and true/neutral headlines is smaller among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims than in the bottom tertile (a positive infotype-by-moderator interaction). The penalty is present in both languages.
design.primaryOutcome: Share: chosen/likely to share the headline (infotype x belief tertile interaction).
design.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, interacted with belief tertile (top vs bottom), with respondent-clustered SEs; language is a secondary stratum.
design.population: Adults in the US, recruited via online panel, in English and Spanish, with quotas by belief tertile.

conditions.title: True/neutral headline
conditions.description: Respondent sees a true or neutral headline.

questions.text: You are invited to a short research survey about how people react to news headlines. Participation is voluntary and you may stop at any time. Do you agree to participate?
How likely do you think each of the following claims is to be true?

rows.text: The 2020 US presidential election was stolen.
A small group of people secretly controls world events.

questions.text: Would you be more likely to share this post?

choices.text: No, I would not share it

questions.text: Based on the available information, do you think this post is likely to be accurate?

Thank you. Some headlines shown in this study were false and were created for research. Please do not share them. Accurate information on these topics is available from public health and fact-checking organizations.

assumptions: Power: about 1300 per arm to detect an interaction of 0.056 at 80% power (S3 misinformation difference 0.056, SE 0.017; interaction MDE exceeds the main-effect MDE of 0.031).
Belief tertiles are computed from the scale mean; quota targets use panel pre-screen data.
Spanish items are professionally translated and back-translated.
Single pre-registered primary test: infotype x top-vs-bottom tertile interaction on share.
unresolved: Actual headline images and Spanish translations must be supplied by the research team.
IRB number, compensation and panel vendor must be set by the research team.
